⏱️Labor Framework, Stages & Arrest Criteria11 items▾

  • ★Highest-yield board sequence for any labor vignette: labor stage / cervical change → fetal tracing → Power–Passenger–Pelvis → intervention → route / timing of delivery.
🧠 Memory toolThe 3 Ps — what to assess when active-phase progress slows
PPower — the uterine contractions
PPassenger — the fetus
PPelvis — the birth canal
In the board sequence the 3 Ps come after labor stage / cervical change and the fetal tracing.
Stages of labor
StageBeginsEndsHigh-yield decisionAnswer
Stage ITrue labor10 cm (complete cervical dilatation)Distinguish latent vs active; active phase ≈ 6 cm onward
Latent phaseLabor onset~6 cmSlow progress alone ≠ cesarean indication
Active phase~6 cm10 cmAssess Power–Passenger–Pelvis if progress slows
Stage II10 cmFetal deliveryAssess descent / rotation; operative vaginal delivery vs CS
Stage IIIFetal deliveryPlacental deliveryActive management; placenta normally separates promptly; >30 min = retained
  • ✎Complete cervical dilatation = . Active labor begins at about — the newer 6-cm threshold is the one explicitly recognised.
Recall
Slow latent phase with a reassuring fetus → cesarean?
tap to flip
Answer
No. Slow progress in the latent phase alone is not an indication for cesarean.
Recall
Active-phase arrest — current criteria?
tap to flip
Answer
≥6 cm + ruptured membranes + no cervical change after 4 h of adequate uterine activity or 6 h of inadequate activity despite oxytocin.
Board trap · The 2-hour arrest rule6 cm + 200 MVU + only 2 h with no change + reassuring fetus ≠ automatic cesarean. The historical 2-hour arrest rule may be too short; waiting 4 or more hours allows many patients to deliver vaginally.
Recall
Third stage: when is the placenta called retained?
tap to flip
Answer
Not delivered after >30 min. Stage III is actively managed and the placenta normally separates promptly.
Recall
Partogram — what is plotted during labor?
tap to flip
Answer
Cervical dilation / descent, contractions, fetal heart rate, membrane status and maternal observations.
Board trap · Stay in scopeLabor and Parturition (8 board items) directly includes no gynecologic entity, FIGO malignancy staging system, menstrual-cycle treatment algorithm or gynecologic screening interval. Do not import FIGO staging or cervical / endometrial / ovarian cancer management into these items — those belong to Gynecologic Oncology.
  • ★Cross-links: contraception / WHO MEC belongs to Contraception and Family Planning — link only postpartum / interpregnancy counseling to a labor vignette when it specifically asks for prevention of rapid repeat pregnancy. Abnormal uterine bleeding staging / evaluation belongs to Abnormalities and diseases affecting the menstrual cycle.

📋Bishop Score, Induction & Elective Timing5 items▾

Bishop score
Component0123Answer
DilatationClosed1–2 cm3–4 cm≥5 cm
Effacement0–30%40–50%60–70%≥80%
Station−3−2−1 / 0≥+1
ConsistencyFirmMediumSoft—
PositionPosteriorMidAnterior—
🧠 Memory toolBishop score — which components reach 3 points
3Dilatation, Effacement, Station — each scored 0 to 3
2Consistency, Position — each scored only 0 to 2
Three numbers go to 3; the two 'feel' items stop at 2.
  • ✎Bishop score : favorable cervix — vaginal delivery after induction is as likely as after spontaneous labor. Bishop : unfavorable — usually needs before induction (ACOG 2009). Classic textbook: ≤5 unfavorable; a score of 7–8 falls between the two definitions.
Board trap · Misoprostol and the scarred uterusAVOID misoprostol for term cervical ripening after prior cesarean / major uterine scar — increased uterine-rupture concern.
Recall
Uncomplicated pregnancy, elective delivery requested — earliest timing?
tap to flip
Answer
Avoid nonmedically indicated delivery before 39 weeks.

💓Uterine Activity & Fetal Heart-Rate Monitoring11 items▾

  • ✎Adequate uterine activity = Montevideo units per 10 min, measured by .
  • ✎Tachysystole = contractions in 10 min, averaged over .
  • ✎Normal FHR baseline = bpm (standard surveillance); fetal tachycardia = bpm.
Recall
Prolonged FHR deceleration — duration (current definition)?
tap to flip
Answer
2 to <10 min.
Recall
Fetal scalp pH — reassuring, indeterminate, nonreassuring?
tap to flip
Answer
>7.25 reassuring (normal)
7.20–7.25 indeterminate
<7.20 nonreassuring
Classic textbook values — fetal scalp sampling is now rarely performed (ACOG 2009).
Three-tier FHR classification
CategoryMeaningKey findingActionAnswer
Category INormalBaseline 110–160 + moderate variability + no late / variable decelerationsContinue surveillance / routine monitoring
Category IIIndeterminateAnything not I or IIICorrect reversible cause(s) + close reassessment
Category III—Absent variability + recurrent late / variable decelerations or bradycardia, OR sinusoidal patternLIFE-SAVING: immediate (urgent) resuscitative measures → expedite delivery if unresolved
Decelerations — cause and implication
DecelerationMechanismImmediate implicationAnswer
EarlyHead compressionUsually physiologic if variability preserved
VariableCord compressionReposition; evaluate cord / oligohydramnios
LateUteroplacental insufficiencyIntrauterine resuscitation — lateral position, stop / reduce oxytocin, correct maternal hypotension / hypoxemia; recurrent late decelerations with absent variability = Category III
🧠 Memory toolVEAL CHOP — FHR pattern → cause
V → CVariable deceleration → Cord compression
E → HEarly deceleration → Head compression
A → OAcceleration → OK (well oxygenated)
L → PLate deceleration → Placental (uteroplacental) insufficiency
Recall
Tachysystole with an abnormal FHR / fetal compromise → response?
tap to flip
Answer
Stop or reduce oxytocin, lateral position, correct maternal hypotension / hypoxemia. Acute uterine relaxation may require terbutaline.
Recall
Sinusoidal FHR pattern → category?
tap to flip
Answer
Category III — on its own, without needing absent variability plus recurrent decelerations / bradycardia.
🩺 Think it through
A laboring woman receiving a uterine stimulant has a Category III tracing that remains uncorrected. What is done first, and what is definitive?
First: stop the uterine stimulant + correct reversible causes. Definitive / life-saving: expedited operative delivery — persistent Category III → expedited delivery.

🔄Malposition, Malpresentation & Breech6 items▾

Malpresentation / dystocia decisions
FindingManagement pearlAnswer
Persistent OP / OTAllow rotation if reassuring → manual / operative rotation if appropriate → CS if failed
Face, mentum anteriorVaginal delivery may be possible
Face, persistent mentum posterior / transverseCesarean
Persistent browUsually CS unless it converts to vertex / face
Transverse lie / shoulderCesarean
Frank / complete breechConsider ECV; selected vaginal delivery only under strict criteria
Footling / incomplete breechHigh cord-prolapse risk; usually CS
Board trap · Face presentation is not automatically cesareanThe chin decides: mentum anterior → vaginal delivery may be possible; persistent mentum posterior / transverse → cesarean.
Recall
Persistent brow presentation → route?
tap to flip
Answer
Usually cesarean, unless it converts to vertex or face.
Recall
Footling / incomplete breech — the feared complication and usual route?
tap to flip
Answer
High risk of cord prolapse; usually cesarean.
  • ✎Persistent breech: external cephalic version at around weeks; if still breech and vaginal-delivery criteria are not met → planned cesarean, commonly at about weeks.
Recall
When is fetal presentation checked — Leopold maneuvers vs ultrasound?
tap to flip
Answer
Leopold maneuvers from around 32–34 wk; ultrasound confirmation at about 35–36 wk when needed.

🚨Shoulder Dystocia & Cord Prolapse7 items▾

  • ✎Shoulder dystocia prevention — consider planned cesarean when EFW is without diabetes or with diabetes.
Shoulder dystocia — life-saving sequence
OrderManeuverAnswer
1Call for help + stop maternal pushing + record time
2McRoberts maneuver
3Suprapubic pressure
4Rubin maneuver
5Woods corkscrew maneuver
6Delivery of the posterior arm
7Repeat maneuvers / Gaskin position ± episiotomy for access
RescueZavanelli maneuver → emergency cesarean
Extreme last resortSymphysiotomy
🧠 Memory toolHELPERR — shoulder dystocia maneuvers
HHelp — call for it
EEvaluate for episiotomy — only for access (in the stepwise sequence it comes late, with Gaskin)
LLegs — McRoberts maneuver
PPressure — suprapubic
EEnter — internal rotation: Rubin, Woods corkscrew
RRemove the posterior arm
RRoll — Gaskin (all-fours) position
FIRST: call for help + McRoberts + suprapubic pressure → definitive / life-saving: internal maneuvers (Rubin / Woods) → posterior arm → Gaskin → rescue maneuvers.
Board trap · Fundal pressureNEVER use fundal pressure in shoulder dystocia. The mechanical goal is to free or rotate the impacted shoulder, not to force the fetus downward.
Recall
Shoulder dystocia — rescue time window?
tap to flip
Answer
Delivery is emphasised within <5 min → escalate maneuvers rapidly.
Recall
Fetal complications of shoulder dystocia?
tap to flip
Answer
Clavicular / humeral fracture, brachial plexus injury / Erb palsy, phrenic injury, hypoxic brain injury, death.
🩺 Think it through
Cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia. What is done first, and what is definitive?
First: elevate the presenting part and relieve cord compression. Definitive / life-saving: emergency cesarean unless immediate vaginal birth is possible — cord prolapse = emergency delivery.

👶Preterm Labor: Diagnosis, Goal of Tocolysis & When Not to Tocolyse6 items▾

Recall
Preterm labor — diagnostic definition?
tap to flip
Answer
Labor (contractions) before 37 weeks + documented cervical change; contractions alone ≠ PTL. 37 weeks is the preterm-birth boundary.
Management: steroids ± tocolysis — tocolysis only when prolonging the pregnancy is appropriate.
Preterm birth by gestational age
ClassGestational ageAnswer
Extremely preterm<28 weeks
Very preterm28 to <32 weeks
Moderate–late preterm32 to <37 weeks
  • ✎Goal of tocolysis: delay delivery about to complete / allow transfer — not weeks, not indefinite prolongation, and never to override a maternal indication for delivery.
🩺 Think it through
Preterm labor at <34 weeks, mother and fetus stable. What is the first action and what is it meant to achieve?
First: antenatal steroid + short-term tocolysis if appropriate (short-term nifedipine). Aim: gain ~48 h for fetal benefit / transfer.
Board trap · Do NOT tocolyse when delivery is indicatedDo not suppress labor merely to prolong an unsafe pregnancy. No tocolysis with: chorioamnionitis / clinical intraamniotic infection / sepsis; significant (major) placental abruption or major hemorrhage; nonreassuring fetal testing / persistent fetal compromise; severe preeclampsia / eclampsia; maternal disease where continuation is unsafe or any other maternal emergency or delivery-required condition. Delaying delivery worsens maternal / fetal danger.
  • ★Delivery timing in PPROM / preterm labor depends on gestational age, infection and fetal status — it is not determined solely by contractions.

💊Tocolytic Drugs & Doses9 items▾

🧠 Memory toolIt's Not My Time — the tocolytics
IIndomethacin — alternative, especially <32 wk
NNifedipine — first-line
MMagnesium sulfate — older textbook alternative; not a first-line tocolytic now
TTerbutaline — restricted alternative; acute rescue, not maintenance
Preterm labor — first-line and alternative tocolytics
DrugStatus / useDoseCritical warningAnswer
NifedipineFIRST-LINE / first-choice agent for short-term tocolysis when appropriate30 mg PO loading → 10–20 mg q4–6 h; max 180 mg/day (current ACOG-based regimen)
Classic textbook: 10 mg PO q15 min during the first hour (until contractions cease) → 10–30 mg q4–6 h		CONTRAINDICATED with significant hypotension / preload-dependent cardiac lesion — maternal hypotension → impaired perfusion, hemodynamic compromise
IndomethacinALTERNATIVE / adjunct, especially (preferably) <32 wk — earlier gestation; other alternatives are institution-specific50–100 mg load → 25–50 mg q4–6 h, for no more than 48 h (current ACOG-based regimen)
Classic textbook: 50 mg PO load → 25 mg q6 h ×48 h		Only <32 wk and only ≤48 h — avoid prolonged / later gestational use; ductus arteriosus constriction + oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypertension; monitor AFI
Magnesium sulfateOlder textbook alternative — not a first-line tocolytic in current guidance (ACOG 2016: first-line = calcium-channel blocker, NSAID or β-agonist)Classic textbook: 6 g IV over 20 min → 2 g/hMonitor DTR / respiratory toxicity; has not clearly improved gestational age at birth
TerbutalineRestricted / selected, historical alternative; acute tachysystole / hypertonus (contraction) rescue0.25 mg SC; classic textbook regimen q20 min ×3, then q3–4 hNot maintenance tocolysis; serious maternal cardiovascular toxicity — tachycardia / tachyarrhythmia, pulmonary edema, ischemia, maternal death; avoid prolonged systemic use — FDA boxed warning (2011): injectable terbutaline not beyond 48–72 h; oral terbutaline contraindicated for preterm labor
  • ✎Nifedipine tocolysis (current ACOG-based regimen): PO loading → q4–6 h; maximum /day. Classic textbook: 10 mg PO q15 min during the first hour (until contractions cease) → 10–30 mg q4–6 h.
Board trap · Nifedipine as a tocolyticCONTRAINDICATED with significant maternal hypotension or a preload-dependent cardiac lesion — hypotension → impaired perfusion / hemodynamic compromise.
  • ✎Indomethacin tocolysis (current ACOG-based regimen): loading → q4–6 h for no more than . Classic textbook: 50 mg PO loading → 25 mg q6 h ×48 h.
Board trap · Indomethacin: the 32-week, short-course rulePrefer <32 weeks and short use only — no more than 48 h (ACOG 2016). AVOID later gestation / prolonged use (particularly ≥32 wk): fetal premature ductus arteriosus constriction, pulmonary hypertension, oligohydramnios (ductal / renal effects). Monitor AFI and stop if amniotic fluid falls.
Recall
Indomethacin — maternal conditions in which it must not be used?
tap to flip
Answer
Significant renal / hepatic dysfunction, GI ulcer disease, platelet dysfunction, aspirin-sensitive asthma → maternal / fetal toxicity.
Recall
Magnesium sulfate as a tocolytic — dose and catch?
tap to flip
Answer
Classic textbook: 6 g IV over 20 min → 2 g/h. Monitor DTR / respiratory toxicity; it has not clearly improved gestational age at birth and is not a first-line tocolytic in current guidance (ACOG 2016).
Recall
Terbutaline — role, dose, and why it is restricted?
tap to flip
Answer
0.25 mg SC for acute tachysystole / hypertonus rescue (classic textbook regimen: q20 min ×3, then q3–4 h). Not maintenance therapy — FDA boxed warning (2011): injectable use not beyond 48–72 h, oral terbutaline contraindicated for preterm labor: tachyarrhythmia, pulmonary edema, ischemia, maternal death.

🧠Antenatal Corticosteroids & Magnesium Neuroprotection8 items▾

Antenatal corticosteroids (fetal maturation)
SteroidDoseRoleNoteAnswer
Betamethasone12 mg IM q24 h ×2 dosesFIRST-LINE antenatal corticosteroid — fetal lung maturationGive when a meaningful preterm-birth risk exists / threatened preterm birth in the appropriate window; ↓ RDS and other prematurity morbidity; not a tocolytic
Dexamethasone6 mg IM q12 h ×4 dosesALTERNATIVE steroidEquivalent accepted regimen / course; not a tocolytic
  • ✎Betamethasone IM q24 h ×; dexamethasone IM q12 h ×4.
Board trap · Steroids buy maturity, not timeAntenatal corticosteroids are not tocolytics. Do not delay an otherwise indicated emergency delivery solely to finish the steroid course.
Recall
Antenatal steroids and tocolysis — <34 wk vs 34 0/7–36 6/7 wk?
tap to flip
Answer
<34 wk: steroid benefit is a major reason to gain the 48-hour window.
34 0/7–36 6/7 wk: benefit from betamethasone is noted, but do not give tocolysis solely to complete steroids.
Recall
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection — when and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Consider when very-preterm delivery is imminent / anticipated — generally, particularly <32 weeks (current guidance) → ↓ risk of cerebral palsy. Dose is protocol based.
Board trap · Magnesium has more than one jobMagnesium for fetal neuroprotection is a different indication from eclampsia, and must not be confused with routine modern first-choice tocolysis.
Board trap · Magnesium sulfate and myasthenia gravisCONTRAINDICATED in myasthenia gravis — neuromuscular weakness / respiratory compromise. Use with caution in renal impairment.
🧠 Memory tool32 weeks — one number, three uses
32Very preterm = 28 to <32 weeks
32Indomethacin — prefer only before 32 weeks
32MgSO₄ neuroprotection — anticipated delivery before 32 weeks

💧PROM & PPROM7 items▾

Recall
PPROM — definition?
tap to flip
Answer
Rupture of membranes before labor and before 37 weeks.
  • ✎Prolonged rupture of membranes = → increased infectious / relevance.
Recall
Suspected rupture of membranes — how is it confirmed?
tap to flip
Answer
Sterile speculum → pooling → nitrazine / ferning.
Equivocal: ultrasound fluid assessment / biochemical test; dye test rarely.
PROM / PPROM rapid decisions
ScenarioBoard actionAnswer
PROM at term (≥37 wk)Induce / augment labor — generally preferred, in most patients
PPROM <34 wk, stable (no infection / fetal compromise)Expectant management + corticosteroids + latency antibiotics (ACOG 2020)
PPROM 34 0/7–36 6/7 wkEither expectant management or immediate delivery / induction is reasonable; expectant management must not go beyond 37 0/7 wk (ACOG 2020)
Classic textbook: deliver at 34 wk
PPROM + chorioamnionitisDELIVER — immediate, regardless of gestational age
PPROM + significant placental abruptionDELIVER — immediate, regardless of gestational age
PPROM + persistent nonreassuring FHR / fetal compromiseDELIVER — immediate, regardless of gestational age
PPROM + cord prolapseEMERGENCY DELIVERY
  • ✎PPROM latency antibiotics (ACOG 2020; 7-day course): IV ampicillin + erythromycin for , then oral amoxicillin + erythromycin for .
Recall
PPROM latency antibiotics — when erythromycin is unavailable or not tolerated?
tap to flip
Answer
Azithromycin once (1 g PO single dose) + IV ampicillin ×48 h → oral amoxicillin ×5 days (ACOG 2020).
🩺 Think it through
PPROM complicated by chorioamnionitis. What is done first, and what must not be done?
First: antibiotics + stabilize. Definitive: delivery. No latency-seeking tocolysis — tocolysis is not used to prolong pregnancy in clinical intraamniotic infection.

🗓️Board Blueprint & Pregnancy Dating10 items▾

  • ★Board weight: 8 items — 2 Understanding | 5 Application | 1 Analysis. The dominant task is selecting the correct test, timing, interpretation, or next intervention.
  • ★Priority sequence of prenatal care: confirm pregnancy → establish dates → baseline maternal screening → aneuploidy/structural screening → maternal metabolic screening → fetal-growth surveillance → delivery planning.
  • ✎Pregnancy is dated as days from the LMP; conceptional age is approximately wk less than gestational age.
Nägele rule (EDD)
EDD = LMP − 3 months + 7 days + 1 year
Use with a certain LMP and regular cycles.
LMP 10 March 2026 → −3 months = 10 December 2025 → +7 days = 17 December 2025 → +1 year = EDD 17 December 2026.
Recall
Known ovulation/conception date → EDD?
tap to flip
Answer
EDD ≈ 266 days after ovulation.
🧠 Memory tool280 vs 266 — which clock is running
280Days from the LMP = gestational age (Nägele rule)
266Days after ovulation/conception → EDD
14The gap: conceptional age runs about 2 wk behind gestational age
Pregnancy dating — which rule applies
ScenarioDating ruleAnswer
Certain LMP + regular cyclesUse LMP and Nägele rule
Uncertain LMP (e.g., positive pregnancy test + uncertain LMP)Ultrasound dating — first-trimester dating US
Discordant uterine size and LMPObtain ultrasound
First-trimester scan availablePrefer the earliest accurate scan
Late scan smaller than established datesDo not automatically redate; evaluate fetal growth
No reliable early datingRecognize increased error in later gestation
Recall
Why must dates be confirmed early?
tap to flip
Answer
Ultrasound dating accuracy decreases as pregnancy advances.
Board trap · Redating a small fetusEstablished early EDD and the fetus measures small on a later scan: the tempting move is to change the due date. Do not automatically redate — the right step is a growth evaluation.
  • ★FIGO malignancy staging does not apply to prenatal care — reserve FIGO staging for gynecologic oncology.

🔬Early Pregnancy Milestones, β-hCG & Fundal Height8 items▾

Recall
Gestational sac on TVUS — when, and what β-hCG discriminatory level?
tap to flip
Answer
About 5 wk. If a discriminatory level is used it should be conservatively high — up to 3,500 mIU/mL (ACOG 2018), so a viable pregnancy is not interrupted.
Classic textbook: 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL.
Recall
Fetal cardiac motion on TVUS — when?
tap to flip
Answer
About 6 wk.
Classic textbook: associated with β-hCG 5,000–6,000 mIU/mL — a rough correlate only, not a diagnostic criterion.
  • ✎Viable early intrauterine pregnancy: minimum β-hCG rise in 48 h is % when the starting level is below 1,500 mIU/mL (40% at 1,500–3,000; 33% above 3,000) (ACOG 2018). Classic textbook: doubles about every 48 h. β-hCG peaks at about wk.
Recall
Fetal heart rate by Doppler — when?
tap to flip
Answer
Approximately 10–14 wk.
Recall
Quickening — when?
tap to flip
Answer
Usually 16–20 wk.

Fundal height ≥3 cm behind or ahead of gestational age (size discrepancy) → next step?

Ultrasound for fetal growth (growth ultrasound) — not an NST: the NST is tempting but it is not the growth test.

Normal pregnancy change vs the finding that signals pathology
SystemNormal pregnancy changeBoard trigger for pathologyAnswer
CardiovascularCardiac output ↑30–50%, SVR ↓, BP falls mid-pregnancyBP above prepregnancy baseline / hypertension
RespiratoryTidal volume ↑30–40%; PaCO₂ about 30 mm Hg by ~20 wkHypoxemia, severe dyspnea, respiratory distress
RenalGFR ↑≈50%; BUN/creatinine fall ~25%A “normal nonpregnant” creatinine may be abnormal
HematologicPlasma volume ↑≈50% > RBC volume ↑20–30% → dilutional anemiaHb/Hct substantially below the pregnancy range
PlateletsMild decline possible<100,000/µL is not physiologic → investigate
WBCMild leukocytosis commonInterpret with clinical evidence of infection
CoagulationHypercoagulableIncreased VTE risk
GIReflux, constipation, slower gastric emptyingPersistent vomiting + weight loss/ketosis
EndocrinehPL → insulin resistanceHyperglycemia → evaluate for GDM
🧠 Memory toolThe “50s” of pregnancy physiology
50Cardiac output rises up to 50% (↑30–50%)
50GFR rises ≈50%
50Plasma volume rises ≈50%
20–30RBC volume lags behind → dilutional anemia
Plasma volume rises more than RBC volume → dilutional anemia.
Board trap · “Normal” creatinineBUN and creatinine fall ~25% in pregnancy because GFR rises ≈50%. A creatinine in the normal nonpregnant range is tempting to dismiss — in pregnancy it may be abnormal.
Board trap · Low plateletsA mild decline is possible, but <100,000/µL is not physiologic — do not label it gestational change; investigate.

Drugs and vaccines to avoid in pregnancy
Drug / classStatusFetal / maternal concernAnswer
Isotretinoin (oral) / systemic retinoidsABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED (isotretinoin; systemic retinoids as a class are also listed as “contraindicated / avoid”)Major teratogen — severe embryopathy: craniofacial, cardiac, CNS, thymic and other malformations
TazaroteneCONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (product labeling; formerly FDA category X) — not used during pregnancy—
Topical tretinoin / adapaleneNot recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding—
MethotrexateABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in a viable (ongoing, intrauterine) desired pregnancyAntimetabolite / antifolate embryotoxicity; abortifacient — fetal loss, congenital anomalies/malformations
MycophenolateCONTRAINDICATED / avoidMajor congenital malformations and pregnancy loss
MifepristoneCONTRAINDICATED in an ongoing desired pregnancy—
WarfarinCONTRAINDICATED for routine pregnancy anticoagulation. Exception: mechanical heart valve — continuing warfarin is reasonable under specialist care when the dose needed is ≤5 mg/day (ACC/AHA 2020)First-trimester warfarin embryopathy → nasal hypoplasia + skeletal abnormalities; CNS/optic abnormalities also reported
ACE inhibitors / ARBsAVOID / contraindicated — discontinue during pregnancyFetal renal injury/dysfunction → oligohydramnios; ACE inhibitors are also associated with congenital anomalies/fetal effects
ValproateAvoid if a safer effective option existsNeural-tube defects + neurodevelopmental injury
Tetracyclines / doxycyclineAVOID in pregnancy, particularly prolonged/later exposureFetal/child teeth and bone toxicity, with later exposure
FluoroquinolonesAvoid in pregnancyUse safer effective pregnancy alternatives when available
NSAIDs / indomethacin in later pregnancyAvoid routine, prolonged or later exposureDuctal constriction; fetal renal effects/oligohydramnios
MMR vaccineCONTRAINDICATED during pregnancyLive attenuated
Varicella vaccineCONTRAINDICATED during pregnancyLive attenuated
Board trap · Not everything is “absolute”Only isotretinoin and methotrexate in a viable desired pregnancy carry the label ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED. Do not mislabel every drug to be avoided (NSAIDs in later pregnancy, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, valproate) as an absolute contraindication.

MethotrexateAntifolate embryotoxicity / fetal loss

🩸Approach to Third-Trimester Bleeding4 items▾

  • ★Exam weight: 5 items — 2 Understanding, 2 Application, 1 Analysis. Work every bleeding case in this order: bleeding pattern → stabilization → diagnosis → fetal status → delivery decision.
Board trap · Elective timing vs emergencyTempting: hold out for the planned gestational age, steroids or more imaging. Right: significant hemorrhage with maternal instability, coagulopathy or fetal compromise overrides elective gestational-age targets — maternal instability always outranks steroids, imaging and elective timing.
Classic presentations — think → immediate next step
PresentationThinkImmediate next stepAnswer
Painless bright-red 3rd-trimester bleedPlacenta previaStabilize + TVUS; NO digital vaginal examination
Painful bleeding + firm/rigid, tender, hypertonic uterusPlacental abruptionStabilize + fetal monitoring + labs
Scarred uterus + sudden pain + bradycardia + loss of stationUterine ruptureLIFE-SAVING: immediate laparotomy
Bleeding after ROM + sinusoidal FHR / bradycardiaRuptured vasa previa — fetal hemorrhage until proven otherwiseLIFE-SAVING: emergency cesarean
Light spotting + friable cervix / visible lesionCervical / vaginal causeSpeculum examination after dangerous obstetric causes are excluded
  • ★Previa type, accreta depth, revealed vs concealed abruption and vasa previa are placental classifications — FIGO staging does not apply (they are not gynecologic cancer stages).

🚫Placenta Previa5 items▾

Placenta previa — current classification (AIUM/ACOG/SMFM 2014)
TypeRelation to internal osBoard implicationAnswer
Placenta previaPlacental edge covers or reaches the internal os, to any degreeCesarean
Low-lying placentaEdge <2 cm from the os, does not cover itRepeat TVUS / individualized route
Classic textbook terms (retired)Complete = covers the entire os; partial = partially covers the os; marginal = edge reaches the osAll three are now simply placenta previa → cesarean; old tables listed marginal as individualized
  • ✎Low-lying placenta = placental edge from the internal os without covering it. Edge 11–20 mm from the os: antepartum hemorrhage risk about and a carefully selected trial of labor may be considered; edge ≤10 mm: bleeding risk far higher (about 29%) and cesarean is usually needed (Vergani 2009; SOGC 2020).
Board trap · Digital examination vs TVUSTempting: check the cervix in a bleeding patient. Right: digital vaginal examination is contraindicated when placenta previa is suspected — transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) is the preferred imaging.
Recall
Low placenta found in the 2nd trimester → follow-up?
tap to flip
Answer
Repeat ultrasound in the 3rd trimester if there is concern for persistence or vasa previa.
Board trap · Indomethacin in bleeding previaAVOID indomethacin in a bleeding placenta previa — platelet inhibition worsens the hemorrhagic concern.

🧲Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS)10 items▾

🧠 Memory toolDepth of invasion in the accreta spectrum
AccretaAdheres — abnormal adherence
IncretaInvades the myometrium
PercretaPenetrates through myometrium/serosa ± bladder/rectum
A → I → P = deeper each step.
Recall
Placenta previa + previous cesarean → assume?
tap to flip
Answer
PAS until excluded, especially an anterior placenta over the scar.
Previa + prior uterine surgery → detailed ultrasound specifically for PAS.
🩺 Think it through
A woman with a prior cesarean and an anterior placenta previa develops hematuria. What is the diagnosis?
Placenta percreta invading the bladder — hematuria + anterior previa + prior CS is the classic vignette.
Recall
Ultrasound clues to PAS?
tap to flip
Answer
Placental lacunae, thin myometrium, absent retroplacental clear zone, abnormal uterovesical vascularity.
Recall
Depth of PAS equivocal on ultrasound → role of MRI?
tap to flip
Answer
Adjunct only — not routine first-line.
Accreta risk when previa coexists with prior cesareans
Prior cesareans (with previa)Accreta riskAnswer
1~3%
2~11%
3~40%
4~61%
5~67%
  • ✎Expected blood loss with placenta accreta: about mL.
Recall
FIRST-LINE operative strategy in extensive PAS — and what must be avoided?
tap to flip
Answer
Cesarean delivery without forcibly removing the placenta → leave placenta in situ → planned hysterectomy.
ABSOLUTELY AVOID forceful/manual placental extraction as a routine maneuver when PAS is strongly suspected — it can precipitate massive hemorrhage.
Recall
Preoperative preparation for PAS?
tap to flip
Answer
Blood products + anesthesia + experienced obstetric surgery ± urology / gynecologic oncology support.
Recall
Postpartum bleeding unresponsive to massage/uterotonics + difficult placental separation → suspect?
tap to flip
Answer
Placenta accreta spectrum.

💥Placental Abruption10 items▾

Recall
Major risk factors for placental abruption?
tap to flip
Answer
Chronic hypertension and preeclampsia.
Recall
Revealed vs concealed abruption?
tap to flip
Answer
Revealed: blood exits through the cervix.
Concealed: blood trapped retroplacentally — about 20% of cases.
Board trap · Normal ultrasoundTempting: exclude abruption because the scan is negative. Right: abruption is primarily a clinical diagnosis; a negative ultrasound does NOT exclude it.
Board trap · Judging by visible bloodMassive blood loss may be concealed and maternal hypotension can appear late — do not rely on visible blood volume alone.
Recall
FIRST-LINE emergency approach to abruption?
tap to flip
Answer
2 large-bore IVs + CBC + type/cross + PT/PTT + fibrinogen + continuous fetal monitoring.
  • ✎In severe abruption, fibrinogen mg/dL marks clinically important hypofibrinogenemia / serious consumptive coagulopathy.
  • ✎Abruption recurrence: about after one prior event and after two — increase surveillance in the next pregnancy.
Recall
Abruption with maternal instability or persistent fetal compromise → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: resuscitation + prompt delivery.
Recall
Abruption: when is cesarean the route?
tap to flip
Answer
Fetus viable, compromised, and vaginal delivery not imminent.
Recall
Abruption with fetal death: why is vaginal delivery preferred?
tap to flip
Answer
When the maternal condition permits, deliver vaginally — surgery in severe coagulopathy can worsen hemorrhage.

⚡Uterine Rupture3 items▾

  • ★Suspected uterine rupture: FIRST resuscitate + activate the operating room → LIFE-SAVING: immediate laparotomy + delivery of the fetus. There is no stable/expectant plan.
  • ✎Risk of rupture/dehiscence with a prior classical cesarean: about %.
Recall
Prior uterine rupture → plan for the next pregnancy?
tap to flip
Answer
Labor should generally be avoided; planned repeat cesarean, commonly at 36–37 wk.

🧵Vasa Previa7 items▾

Recall
Vasa previa — definition, plan, and the contraindicated procedure?
tap to flip
Answer
Unprotected fetal vessels over/near the internal os → planned cesarean.
ABSOLUTELY AVOID — contraindicated: artificial rupture of membranes in known vasa previa → rupture of the fetal vessels.
  • ✎Vasa previa incidence ≈ . Fetal blood volume ≈ mL/kg; fetal-vessel rupture carries perinatal mortality of about %.
Recall
Risk factors for vasa previa?
tap to flip
Answer
Velamentous cord insertion, succenturiate/bilobed placenta, IVF, multiple gestation, previous low-lying placenta.
Recall
Best antepartum test for vasa previa?
tap to flip
Answer
TVUS with color Doppler when risk factors are identified — including follow-up of a low-lying placenta or succenturiate lobe.

LIFE-SAVING: emergency cesarean with the neonatal team prepared for transfusion.

🚨First-Trimester Bleeding: First Moves6 items▾

Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Stable or unstable? Assess maternal stability first.

tap to flip

Resuscitate + urgently evaluate for ruptured ectopic → LIFE-SAVING surgery.

Quantitative β-hCG + TVUS.

💉Ectopic Pregnancy & Methotrexate7 items▾

Recall
TVUS discriminatory β-hCG level — and what if no definite IUP is seen in a stable patient?
tap to flip
Answer
If a discriminatory level is used, set it conservatively high — as high as 3,500 mIU/mL (ACOG 2018). Classic textbook: ≈1,500–2,000 mIU/mL.
No definite IUP + stable → serial β-hCG/TVUS, not automatic methotrexate.
  • ✎MTX-favorable ectopic (stable, reliable patient): β-hCG < mIU/mL, mass no larger than cm (ACOG 2018: >4 cm on TVUS is a relative contraindication; some protocols use <3.5 cm), no fetal cardiac activity → consider the FIRST-LINE medical option: methotrexate IM.
  • ✎After MTX for ectopic: check β-hCG on day and day ; a decline of ≥% from day 4 → 7 = adequate response → continue weekly β-hCG until negative (<5 mIU/mL); a fall <15% → additional treatment (retreat / reassess).
🧠 Memory toolMethotrexate for ectopic — the numbers in order

4 cmmass no larger than this
0fetal cardiac activity
50mg/m² IM
4 → 7days of β-hCG checks
15%minimum fall between them
<5mIU/mL = stop weekly follow-up
5,000 – 4 – 0 to qualify, 50 to treat, 4–7–15 to judge the response.
Board trap · MTX in the unstable patientHemodynamically unstable or ruptured ectopic + methotrexate → CONTRAINDICATED as management. Tempting because the patient "has an ectopic"; right answer: surgery is life-saving.
Board trap · MTX with a viable desired IUPMethotrexate is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in a viable desired intrauterine pregnancy and is not continued in pregnancy: antifolate / antimetabolite → embryotoxicity, pregnancy loss, anomalies. It is used intentionally for ectopic pregnancy and GTN.
Recall
Mifepristone — status in an ongoing desired pregnancy?
tap to flip
Answer
CONTRAINDICATED in an ongoing desired pregnancy.

tap to flip

Maternal malnutrition → impaired fetal growth if prolonged.

tap to flip

hCG should fall; plateau / rise → GTN.

📈Approach & Antenatal Fetal Testing (NST, BPP, Doppler)8 items▾

  • ★PLE decision sequence: confirm dating → define the presentation/growth abnormality → assess fetal reserve → determine whether surveillance or delivery is safer.
Recall
Future contraception after malpresentation / macrosomia / IUGR — chosen according to what?
tap to flip
Answer
The underlying maternal condition (diabetes, hypertension, obesity, renal disease, autoimmune disease) — not the fetal size/presentation diagnosis itself.
Recall
Reduced fetal movement in a viable fetus → best next step?
tap to flip
Answer
NST / BPP.
  • ✎Reactive NST (reassuring) = or more accelerations in min, each ≥ bpm lasting ≥15 sec — "2 × 15 × 15 in 20".
Recall
Reassuring BPP score?
tap to flip
Answer
8–10 / 10.
  • ✎Antenatal fetal surveillance for high-risk disease commonly begins at weeks, depending on the condition.
FHR / umbilical artery (UA) Doppler — rapid interpretation
FindingInterpretationImplicationAnswer
Late decelerationUteroplacental insufficiencyParticularly important in IUGR
Reduced (decreased) UA diastolic flowIncreased placental resistanceIntensify surveillance
Absent end-diastolic flowAbnormal — severe placental dysfunction (more severe placental insufficiency)Delivery may be required
Reversed end-diastolic flowAbnormal — severe placental dysfunction; highest concern; very high IUFD / acidemia riskStrong delivery trigger — escalated surveillance / delivery decision
Recall
UA Doppler abnormality detected → what happens to the Doppler schedule?
tap to flip
Answer
Repeat more frequently once an abnormality is detected.

🔄Breech Presentation & External Cephalic Version6 items▾

Breech types
TypePositionDelivery implicationAnswer
FrankHips flexed, knees extendedSelected vaginal breech may be considered
CompleteHips and knees flexedSelected vaginal breech may be considered
Incomplete / footlingOne or both feet/knees below the breechRelative contraindication to vaginal breech — cesarean favored / generally recommended
🧠 Memory toolBreech timeline — weeks to remember
32–34Begin Leopold maneuvers for fetal presentation
35–36Ultrasound to confirm presentation (routine or if presentation questionable)
≥37ECV for persistent breech, if appropriate — offered from 37 0/7 wk onward (ACOG 2020). Classic textbook: 37–38 wk
~39Classic textbook: repeat ECV after a failed first attempt, under regional (spinal/epidural) anesthesia — neuraxial analgesia with a tocolytic raises ECV success (ACOG 2020)
Breech → ECV from 37 wk → failed → repeat attempt (classically ~39 wk under regional anesthesia) → failed again → cesarean commonly.
Recall
Second ECV attempt fails → delivery plan?
tap to flip
Answer
Cesarean delivery is commonly recommended.
Recall
Patient with persistent breech declines ECV → plan?
tap to flip
Answer
Planned cesarean after 39 wk.
Recall
Who may have a selected vaginal breech trial?
tap to flip
Answer
Frank or complete breech meeting strict criteria: flexed head + adequate pelvis + EFW within the selected range — and only with an experienced provider / setting.
Board trap · Vaginal breech EFW range — no single cutoffClassic textbook criterion for selected vaginal breech: EFW 2,000–3,800 g; the vignette version is 2,500–3,800 g — the vignette cutoff (2,500–3,800 g) is likely testable. Current guidance (ACOG 2018) fixes no single weight range: planned vaginal breech may be reasonable only under a hospital-specific protocol for eligibility and labor management, with an experienced provider.

👶Face, Brow, Transverse Lie & Compound Presentation2 items▾

Other malpresentations — critical rule
PresentationRuleAnswer
Face — mentum anteriorVaginal delivery may occur
Face — persistent mentum posterior / transverseMust rotate anteriorly or cesarean (cesarean unless rotation occurs)
BrowUsually must convert to vertex or face to deliver
Transverse lie / shoulderPersistent presentation → cesarean
Compound — upper extremityMay retract/reduce; monitor for cord prolapse
Compound — lower extremity with vertexVaginal delivery much less likely
Recall
Face presentation: which chin position can deliver vaginally?
tap to flip
Answer
Mentum anterior = vaginal delivery possible.
Persistent mentum posterior (or transverse) = cesarean unless it rotates anteriorly.

Large fetus — cutoffs and delivery rule
Condition / decisionCutoffBoard implicationAnswer
LGABirth weight ≥90th percentile for gestational age (ACOG 2020). Classic textbook: EFW >90th percentileEvaluate diabetes, obesity, dating
MacrosomiaBirth weight above 4,000 g or 4,500 g regardless of gestational age — no universal cutoff (ACOG 2020). Classic textbook: >4,500 gIncreased birth trauma / cesarean risk
Planned CS, no diabetesEFW ≥5,000 g (ACOG 2020)Elective cesarean may be considered
Planned CS, diabetesEFW ≥4,500 g (ACOG 2020)Elective cesarean may be considered
🧠 Memory toolMacrosomia numbers — 4,500 does double duty
4,500 gClassic textbook macrosomia cutoff (birth weight above this; 4,000 g is also used); EFW at/above this = consider cesarean if diabetic
5,000 gEFW at/above this = consider cesarean when there is no diabetes
Diabetes lowers the cesarean threshold by 500 g.
  • ✎Ultrasound EFW is accurate only to about ±% — do not treat it as the exact weight.
Board trap · Shoulder dystocia is unpredictableTempting: "no macrosomia, so no shoulder dystocia." Macrosomia raises the risk, but many shoulder dystocias occur below the classic macrosomic weight thresholds — it remains an unpredictable intrapartum emergency.

📉SGA & Fetal Growth Restriction (IUGR)9 items▾

  • ✎FGR = ultrasound EFW or abdominal circumference below the percentile for gestational age; SGA = newborn birth weight below the 10th percentile (ACOG 2021). Classic textbook: SGA = EFW below the 10th percentile. Risk rises below the and especially the percentile (greater morbidity/mortality; EFW below the 3rd = severe FGR).
Recall
Fetus with EFW below the 10th percentile — what must be distinguished?
tap to flip
Answer
Constitutional smallness vs pathological FGR.
Growth restriction — patterns
ClassificationPatternTypical interpretationAnswer
Symmetric FGRHead, abdomen and long bones proportionately smallEarlier insult, commonly before 20 wk
Asymmetric FGRRelative head sparing + small abdomen/torsoLater uteroplacental insufficiency
Constitutional SGASmall but maintains the expected growth trajectoryOften normal Doppler / testing
Pathologic FGRFalls progressively off the growth curveRequires intensified surveillance
🧠 Memory toolSymmetric vs asymmetric FGR
SymmetricSoon — earlier insult (commonly before 20 wk); everything proportionately small
AsymmetricAfter — later uteroplacental insufficiency; head spared, abdomen small
Classic textbook contrast pair. Current guidance (SMFM 2020) classifies FGR by onset instead — early (diagnosed before 32 wk) vs late (32 wk or later); the symmetric/asymmetric pattern does not independently predict outcome.
Recall
Maternal hypertensive disease → which fetal growth complication, and by what mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Chronic hypertension and preeclampsia → uteroplacental insufficiency → IUGR/FGR.
  • ✎Fundal height is screened at prenatal visits after about wk; a difference of more than cm from gestational age in weeks → growth ultrasound.
  • ✎FGR surveillance: serial growth ultrasound every wk — never more often than every 2 wk (ACOG 2021); classic textbook: every 2–3 wk. NST/BPP often , depending on severity.
FGR (IUGR) — delivery timing (ACOG 2021 / SMFM 2020)
SituationRuleAnswer
Reassuring testing + normal Doppler, EFW 3rd to below 10th percentileContinue surveillance toward term → deliver at 38 0/7–39 0/7 wk
Normal Doppler, EFW below 3rd percentile (severe FGR)Deliver at 37 wk
Decreased UA diastolic flow (not absent/reversed)Deliver at 37 wk
Absent end-diastolic flowDeliver early — 33 0/7–34 0/7 wk
Reversed end-diastolic flowDeliver early — 30 0/7–32 0/7 wk
Nonreassuring NST / BPPDeliver — earlier than the windows above, according to fetal/maternal status
Preterm delivery anticipatedGive antenatal corticosteroids when feasible
🩺 Think it through
A preterm growth-restricted fetus under surveillance now shows absent end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. What is the plan?
Think delivery: with absent end-diastolic flow deliver at 33–34 wk (reversed flow: 30–32 wk), earlier if fetal testing becomes nonreassuring or maternal status worsens, and give antenatal corticosteroids when feasible. Normal Doppler + reassuring testing would instead mean continued surveillance toward term.

🩸Rh-Negative Mother: RhIG & Alloimmunization2 items▾

  • ✎Rh-negative, unsensitized mother: routine Rho(D) immune globulin at about wk, plus after sensitizing events and postpartum as indicated.
Board trap · Already sensitized Rh-negative motherTempting: give RhIG. Right: once the mother is already sensitized, do not rely on RhIG → monitor alloimmunization / fetal anemia.

🩺Diagnostic Cut-offs & Severe Features6 items▾

  • ★Exam approach: BP cut-off → classify the disorder → identify severe features → give MgSO₄ / antihypertensive if indicated → determine delivery timing.
Numeric cut-offs to memorize
FindingCut-offMeaning / actionAnswer
Hypertension in pregnancy (gestational HTN / preeclampsia)≥140/90 mm Hg on 2 measurements ≥4 h apart, after 20 wkGestational HTN if no preeclampsia features; preeclampsia if + proteinuria / end-organ disease
Severe-range BP≥160 systolic and/or ≥110 diastolicConfirm within 15 min; if it persists ≥15 min give an antihypertensive as soon as possible, within 30–60 min (ACOG 2020)
24-h urine protein≥300 mg/24 hSignificant proteinuria — supports preeclampsia; manage by severe features
Protein/creatinine ratio≥0.3Supports preeclampsia
Urine dipstick2+ (ACOG 2020)Only when quantitative methods are unavailable. Classic textbook: +1
Platelets<100,000/µLSevere feature (severe thrombocytopenia)
Creatinine>1.1 mg/dL or doubling of baseline (no other renal disease)Severe renal feature
AST/ALT (transaminases)≥2× normal (upper limit)Severe hepatic feature
  • ✎Hypertension in pregnancy = BP ≥ mm Hg on readings at least h apart, after 20 wk.
  • ✎Proteinuria of preeclampsia = ≥ mg/24 h or protein/creatinine ratio ≥.
🧠 Memory toolSevere features of preeclampsia — number hook “100 · 1.1 · 2× · lungs · head”
100Platelets <100,000/µL
1.1Creatinine >1.1 mg/dL or doubled baseline
2×Transaminases (AST/ALT) ≥2× normal
LungsPulmonary edema
HeadCerebral / visual symptoms
Any one of these (or BP ≥160/110) = preeclampsia with severe features.
Recall
Urine dipstick as the proteinuria criterion — what reading, and when may it be used?
tap to flip
Answer
2+ (ACOG 2020), and only when quantitative methods (24-h protein, P/C ratio) are unavailable. Classic textbook: +1.

🗂️Classifying the Hypertensive Disorders7 items▾

Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy — classification
DisorderDiagnostic coreProteinuria / severe featuresManagementAnswer
Gestational HTNNew HTN after 20 wk: ≥140/90 ×2, ≥4 h apartNo proteinuria; no severe featuresSurveillance
Preeclampsia without severe featuresSame BP criterion (≥140/90 ×2, ≥4 h apart, after 20 wk) + proteinuriaProteinuria ≥300 mg/24 h or P/C ≥0.3; no severe featuresSurveillance
Preeclampsia with severe featuresSevere BP ≥160/110 OR hypertension + a qualifying severe end-organ findingPlatelets <100,000; Cr >1.1 or doubled baseline; AST/ALT ≥2×; pulmonary edema; cerebral (neurologic)/visual symptoms. Proteinuria may be absentMgSO₄ + urgent BP control
EclampsiaPreeclampsia (PE spectrum) + new-onset, otherwise unexplained generalized tonic-clonic seizureThe seizure itself defines the syndrome; proteinuria variableLife-saving MgSO₄ → stabilize → deliver
Chronic HTNHTN before conception, or before 20 wk, or persisting >6 wk postpartumVariableControl BP + surveillance
Superimposed preeclampsiaChronic HTN + new/worsening proteinuria or end-organ injury± severe features—
HELLPHemolysis + elevated liver enzymes + low platelets (thrombocytopenia)Severe disease—
Board trap · Waiting for proteinuriaPreeclampsia with severe features does not need proteinuria: severe BP ≥160/110 or one severe organ feature is enough — proteinuria may be absent.
Recall
What single event turns preeclampsia into eclampsia?
tap to flip
Answer
A new-onset generalized (tonic-clonic) seizure not explained by another cause — the seizure itself defines the syndrome.
Chronic HTN vs superimposed preeclampsia
FeatureChronic HTNSuperimposed PEAnswer
TimingBefore pregnancy / <20 wk / >6 wk postpartumUsually after 20 wk
BPPre-existingWorsens
ProteinuriaMay be present at baselineNew or increasing
24-h proteinBaseline measurement neededNew ≥300 mg/24 h supports PE
End-organ featuresChronic disease possibleNew severe PE features
Uric acid (adjunct)Variable>6.0–6.5 may support the diagnosis
Fetal riskIUGR, prematurityHigher IUGR / abruption risk
  • ✎Chronic HTN = hypertension before conception, before wk, or persisting beyond wk postpartum.
Recall
Chronic hypertensive develops new or worsening proteinuria / end-organ disease → diagnosis?
tap to flip
Answer
Superimposed preeclampsia. New proteinuria ≥300 mg/24 h clearly supports it. Proteinuria may already be present at baseline, so a baseline 24-h urine protein at the initial visit is needed to recognize new or increasing proteinuria.
Recall
Baseline renal disease makes proteinuria hard to interpret — which adjunct lab may support superimposed PE?
tap to flip
Answer
Uric acid >6.0–6.5 mg/dL.

🚨Eclampsia — The Emergency Sequence6 items▾

  • ★LIFE-SAVING sequence — pregnant patient seizing: ABCs → magnesium sulfate immediately (recurrent seizure → additional MgSO₄) → urgent control of severe BP ≥160/110 → stabilize the mother → deliver.
Eclampsia — emergency drug card
PriorityTherapyDose / ruleAnswer
LIFE-SAVING — FIRST (immediate)ABCs, maternal stabilizationProtect airway, oxygenation (breathing), circulation; lateral positioning; protect from injury. Stabilization precedes delivery
FIRST-LINE anticonvulsant (life-saving)Magnesium sulfate4–6 g IV over 20–30 min → 1–2 g/h infusion (ACOG 2020). Classic textbook: 6 g IV over 15–20 min → 2 g/h
Recurrent seizureAdditional MgSO₄2 g IV over 3–5 min; continue seizure precautions; do not substitute immediate delivery for initial seizure control
Refractory / status seizuresLorazepam / phenytoin / phenobarbitalAlternatives only — not first-line
Severe BPIV labetalol, IV hydralazine or immediate-release PO nifedipineTreat ≥160/110 persisting ≥15 min urgently — within 30–60 min (ACOG 2020), after seizure control/stabilization; reduce BP below the severe range
Mg toxicity antidoteCalcium gluconate10 mL of 10% solution (1 g) IV over about 3 min (ACOG 2020)
DEFINITIVE therapyDeliveryOnly after seizure control and maternal stabilization — not the first maneuver during an active seizure
CesareanNot automaticOnly for an obstetric indication or nonresolving fetal compromise; route is based on obstetric indication
  • ✎Eclampsia: MgSO₄ g IV over 20–30 min → g/h infusion (ACOG 2020); recurrent seizure → additional g IV over 3–5 min. Classic textbook: 6 g over 15–20 min → 2 g/h.
Board trap · Phenytoin firstPhenytoin is NOT first-line for routine eclampsia — MgSO₄ is preferred. Phenytoin, phenobarbital and lorazepam are alternatives reserved for refractory seizures / status.
Board trap · “Deliver immediately” / rush to cesareanCesarean is not the first treatment of an actively seizing patient, and eclampsia alone is not a reason to operate while the mother is still seizing/uncontrolled. “Deliver immediately” is wrong if she is unstable: stabilize first → then deliver.
Recall
After the initial magnesium regimen, how many eclamptic patients convulse again?
tap to flip
Answer
About 10% have a second convulsion.

💉Magnesium Sulfate — Prophylaxis, Levels & Toxicity7 items▾

  • ✎Seizure prophylaxis in severe preeclampsia (first-line): MgSO₄ g IV loading → g/h, continued through about h postpartum (same postpartum duration after eclampsia; HELLP likewise gets MgSO₄ seizure prophylaxis through about 24 h postpartum).
Board trap · Magnesium for everyonePreeclampsia without severe features: routine MgSO₄ prophylaxis is not recommended.
Board trap · Magnesium is not an antihypertensiveMgSO₄ is for seizure prophylaxis/treatment — it is not a BP drug. Severe BP still needs labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine.
Board trap · Magnesium contraindicationAVOID MgSO₄ in myasthenia gravis (standard board-review point). In renal failure, reduce the dose and monitor carefully.
Serum magnesium levels (mg/dL) — therapeutic range and toxicity ladder
Serum MgClinical effectActionAnswer
4.8–8.4 mg/dLTherapeutic range for seizure prophylaxis—
~10 mg/dLLoss of deep tendon reflexesStop Mg, evaluate
~15 mg/dLRespiratory depression / paralysisEmergency
20–25 mg/dLCardiac arrestCritical toxicity
🧠 Memory toolMagnesium toxicity ladder — number hook “5 · 10 · 15 · 20+”
~5–8Therapeutic (4.8–8.4)
10Reflexes lost (DTRs) → stop Mg, evaluate
15Respiration depressed / paralysis
20–25Cardiac arrest
Order of loss: reflexes → respiration → heart.
  • ✎Magnesium toxicity antidote: calcium gluconate mL of % solution ( g) IV over about 3 min.

💊Antihypertensives — Acute Severe BP & Chronic Therapy9 items▾

Acute severe hypertension (≥160/110) — first-line options (ACOG 2020)
DrugStandard board doseNoteAnswer
IV labetalol20 mg IV → 40 mg after 10 min → 80 mg after another 10 min if neededFirst-line; treat ≥160/110 mm Hg persisting ≥15 min, within 30–60 min
IV hydralazine5–10 mg IV, repeat according to responseFirst-line — all three agents are equally first-line; avoid maternal hypotension
Immediate-release nifedipine PO10 mg PO → 20 mg if severe BP persistsFirst-line oral option — equally first-line; use when IV access is delayed
  • ★The classic textbook names IV labetalol, IV hydralazine and PO nifedipine as the acute options without giving an exact dosing sequence; the doses above are standard board-review material. Choose the agent by contraindications and availability.
  • ✎Acute severe BP: labetalol mg IV → mg → mg, each step 10 min apart, if still severe.
Recall
LIFE-SAVING purpose of treating BP ≥160/110 urgently?
tap to flip
Answer
Prevent maternal stroke / cerebral hemorrhage (and do not delay an indicated delivery).
Recall
Target of acute antihypertensive treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
Bring BP below the severe range (<160/110).
Recall
Severe BP and IV access is delayed → which drug?
tap to flip
Answer
Immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg PO (→ 20 mg if severe BP persists) — the oral option.
Board trap · Waiting 4 hours to confirmThe ≥4-h interval is for diagnosis. Once BP ≥160/110 is persistent/severe, do not delay treatment waiting for 4-hour confirmation.
Board trap · Over-correcting the BPAvoid excessive BP reduction / severe maternal hypotension — it can worsen uteroplacental perfusion.
Which drug for which job
DrugRolePositionAnswer
LabetalolChronic HTNCommonly used agent
NifedipineChronic HTNCommonly used agent
HydralazineAcute severe HTNIV emergency agent
MgSO₄Seizure prophylaxisNot a BP drug
Low-dose aspirinPrevention81 mg/day, started at 12–28 wk (ideally before 16 wk) in high-risk patients, until delivery (ACOG 2021)

⏰Delivery Timing5 items▾

When to deliver
ConditionDelivery ruleAnswer
Gestational HTN (without severe features)37 wk
Preeclampsia without severe features37 wk
Preeclampsia with severe features34 wk if maternal/fetal status is stable (after MgSO₄ + BP treatment); sooner for deterioration
Severe features <34 wkExpectant inpatient management to 34 wk only if mother and fetus are stable

37Gestational HTN and preeclampsia without severe features

Recall
LIFE-SAVING rule: which conditions override routine gestational-age targets?
tap to flip

Eclampsia, uncontrolled severe hypertension, HELLP deterioration, pulmonary edema, DIC, abruption, AFLP, or persistent fetal compromise.
Recall
Severe preeclampsia before 34 wk — when is expectant management allowed, and where?
tap to flip
Answer
Only while mother and fetus remain stable, and only as an inpatient, up to 34 wk.
Board trap · Tocolysis to buy timeIn preeclampsia/eclampsia requiring delivery, do not use tocolysis to postpone a medically necessary birth.

🩸HELLP Syndrome & AFLP7 items▾

🧠 Memory toolHELLP — what the letters mean and how each shows up
HHemolysis — schistocytes, ↑LDH, ↑bilirubin

RUQ / epigastric pain, with nausea/vomiting.

🩺 Think it through
A woman with HELLP before 34 wk is stable; betamethasone is given with delivery planned 24–48 h later. Her liver injury then worsens rapidly and DIC develops. Do you wait to complete the steroid course?
No — deliver immediately. LIFE-SAVING: rapidly worsening liver injury, DIC, fetal compromise, severe uncontrolled HTN or risk of hepatic rupture → do not delay delivery for steroid completion.
  • ✎HELLP perinatal outcome: stillbirth rate %; neonatal mortality %.

⛔Drugs to Avoid, PPH Pairing & Contraception6 items▾

Board trap · ACE inhibitors / ARBsCONTRAINDICATED — avoid / discontinue in pregnancy (standard board-review rule). The established harm is second- and third-trimester fetal renal injury/failure → oligohydramnios; an association of ACE inhibitors with congenital anomalies has also been reported but is less well established.
Board trap · Methylergonovine in the hypertensive patientABSOLUTELY AVOID methylergonovine (0.2 mg IM) in HTN / preeclampsia — severe hypertension and vasoconstriction. It is only an alternative uterotonic and is contraindicated here. Preeclampsia + postpartum hemorrhage → oxytocin first; never choose methylergonovine as the uterotonic (it should not be given if another uterotonic is suitable).
Contraception after a hypertensive pregnancy
MethodRelevance to hypertensionAnswer
Copper IUDNo hypertension-specific restriction
LNG-IUDGenerally appropriate
ImplantGenerally appropriate
Progestin-only pillGenerally appropriate
DMPACaution increases with severe HTN / vascular disease (standard board-review point)
Combined estrogen-progestinWHO MEC 4 with severe HTN ≥160/100 or vascular disease (standard board-review point)
  • ✎Combined estrogen-progestin contraception is WHO MEC category with severe hypertension ≥ or vascular disease.
  • ★Hypertension itself does not require delaying contraception; choose the method according to postpartum status, BP severity, vascular disease, breastfeeding and VTE risk.
  • ★FIGO oncologic staging is not applicable to hypertension in pregnancy.

tap to flip
Answer
The White classification, especially A1/A2 and F/R/RF/H/T. FIGO malignancy staging is not applicable to diabetes.

Why is the newborn of a diabetic mother hypoglycemic?
tap to flip
Answer
Maternal hyperglycemia → fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia; fetal insulin persists after cord clamping → neonatal hypoglycemia.

Hyperglycemia during organogenesis → which anomalies?
tap to flip

Cardiac defects, neural tube defects, and caudal regression.

tap to flip

Diabetes substantially raises preeclampsia risk, so BP and protein surveillance are part of diabetic prenatal care.
Recall
DKA in a diabetic pregnancy → what does management require?
tap to flip
Answer
Medical emergency: IV fluids, insulin, electrolyte correction, and fetal/maternal monitoring. Ketoacidosis is listed among the maternal complications of diabetes, but no complete DKA dosing protocol is given — do not invent one.

Recall
First-line treatment of GDM, before any drug?
tap to flip
Answer
Diabetic diet + (mild) exercise + glucose monitoring — glucose checked four times/day: fasting + three postprandial values.
  • ✎Postmeal walking in GDM: about min, beginning min after eating.
Recall
GDM on diet/exercise — when is medication started?
tap to flip
Answer
When glucose targets are not consistently met despite diet/exercise → class A2 → medication (insulin). If targets are met → stays A1.
ACOG 2018 sets no fixed percentage. Classic textbook: more than 25–30% of values elevated.

💉GDM Pharmacotherapy7 items▾

GDM drugs: first-line vs alternative vs not first-line
CategoryAgentKey pointAnswer
FIRST-LINE pharmacologicInsulinIndividualized to the fasting/postprandial glucose pattern; typical starting total 0.7–1.0 U/kg/day in divided doses (ACOG 2018), then titrated — no universal fixed dose
Insulin patternShort-acting lispro/aspart + intermediate NPHAdjusted according to the glucose pattern
ALTERNATIVE (second-line)MetforminSelected patients: when insulin is refused, cannot be used or is not feasible. Crosses the placenta; long-term outcome data limited/uncertain

Recall
GDM requiring medication → FIRST-LINE drug?
tap to flip
Answer
Insulin — dose individualized to the glucose profile (short-acting lispro/aspart + NPH).
Recall
Key safety advantage of insulin over oral agents in pregnancy?
tap to flip
Answer
Insulin does not cross the placenta. Oral agents such as metformin have been studied, but insulin remains favored.
Board trap · Fixed GDM insulin doseTempting: give every woman one fixed insulin dose. Right: there is no universal fixed insulin dose for GDM — ACOG 2018 gives only a typical starting total of 0.7–1.0 U/kg/day in divided doses, which is then titrated to the fasting/postprandial pattern with short- and intermediate-acting insulin. Unlike eclampsia or PPH, uncomplicated GDM has no single emergency bolus dose.
  • ✎When insulin is started for GDM, the typical starting total is U/kg/day in divided doses (ACOG 2018), then titrated. Classic textbook: U/kg is the regimen described for established diabetes.
Board trap · Glyburide / metformin "contraindicated"Neither is absolutely contraindicated. Glyburide is simply not first-line (short-term outcomes worse than with insulin). Metformin is second-line (crosses the placenta; long-term outcome data limited).
🩺 Think it through
A woman with GDM still has more than 25–30% of her glucose values above target despite diet and exercise, and she will not take insulin. What is offered?
Metformin — the alternative when insulin is declined or not feasible. Insulin remains first-line; glyburide is not first-line.

⚡Seizures & Epilepsy in Pregnancy8 items▾

Board trap · New seizure after 20 weeksTempting: treat an unexplained seizure at ≥20 wk as routine epilepsy. Do not treat as routine epilepsy first — seizure after 20 wk + hypertensive features → MgSO₄ first (give MgSO₄ if eclampsia is clinically compatible). Management of a known seizure disorder is explicitly distinguished from eclampsia, for which magnesium is used.
Recall
Known epilepsy with an acute seizure in pregnancy → anticonvulsant approach?
tap to flip
Answer
Continue/restore the AED; IV phenytoin or a benzodiazepine when required.
  • ★Epilepsy in pregnancy: do not abruptly stop the AED → prefer effective monotherapy → folic acid at least 0.4 mg/day before conception and through pregnancy (AAN/AES/SMFM 2024); 4 mg/day if on valproate or carbamazepine or with a prior NTD (ACOG 2017) → total/free AED concentration approximately monthly → NTD screening by detailed (targeted) fetal anatomy scan at 19–20 wk, now the primary screen (ACOG 2017); MSAFP at 15–20 wk is the classic adjunct.
    Classic textbook: folate 4 mg/day for all women with epilepsy.
  • ✎Antenatal maternal vitamin K for enzyme-inducing AEDs is : insufficient evidence that it prevents newborn bleeding (AAN 2009); the newborn receives routine vitamin K mg IM at birth. Classic textbook: optional maternal oral vitamin K 10 mg/day in the last month (from 36 wk).
Board trap · ValproateValproate (valproic acid): AVOID when an effective safer AED is available — strong neural-tube-defect and neurodevelopmental risk (plus other congenital defects).
Recall
Carbamazepine in pregnancy — fetal risk and board rule?
tap to flip
Answer
Neural-tube defects (risk lower than with valproate, which carries the highest risk). Use only when clinically appropriate rather than abruptly stopping seizure control.
Recall
Maternal generalized seizure → effect on the fetus?
tap to flip
Answer
Maternal hypoxia/trauma → fetal hypoxia/bradycardia.
Recall
Controlled epilepsy → when to deliver?
tap to flip
Answer
No specific indication for early delivery; routine obstetric timing.

  • ✎Treated hypothyroidism: keep TSH in the lower half of the trimester-specific range; if no such range is available, below mIU/L (ATA 2017). Classic textbook: about 0.5–2.5 mIU/L throughout pregnancy.
  • ✎Hypothyroid patient becomes pregnant → levothyroxine dose ↑ .
  • ✎Thyroid disorder monitoring: TSH ± free T4 every wk / at least each .

tap to flip

TSI (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin), when relevant.

tap to flip

Watch for fetal goiter/tachycardia: detailed ultrasound at about 18–20 wk, repeat in the 3rd trimester; later fetal surveillance.

Goiter appears in both: fetal hyperthyroidism with maternal TSI, fetal hypothyroidism with excess antithyroid drug.

tap to flip

Neurodevelopmental impairment.

tap to flip

Routine obstetric timing.

Board trap · WarfarinWarfarin: AVOID in pregnancy — contraindicated for routine pregnancy anticoagulation (teratogen; heparin is used instead). Do not call it a universal absolute: a mechanical heart valve is the specialist exception — warfarin may be continued when the daily dose is <5 mg, through the 2nd and 3rd trimesters until 36 wk, then changed to heparin in hospital (ESC 2018), under a specialist protocol.
Recall
Warfarin in pregnancy — classic fetal effects?
tap to flip
Answer
Embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia + skeletal abnormalities; CNS abnormalities/optic atrophy; fetal bleeding.

🔪Appendicitis in Pregnancy3 items▾

tap to flip

Ultrasound → MRI if nondiagnostic → appendectomy when confirmed/highly suspected.

tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING: urgent operative control of the infectious focus + IV antibiotics.
🩺 Think it through
A woman in late pregnancy with a viable fetus has perforated appendicitis with peritonitis. The team debates delivering her first. What comes first?
Maternal control of the infectious focus comes first; deliver only for an obstetric/fetal indication. Appendicitis carries no automatic delivery — operate when indicated regardless of trimester.

🧠 Memory toolTrauma primary sequence — ABCs
AAirway
BBreathing
CCirculation

  • ✎Significant trauma + viable fetus: continuous FHR/uterine monitoring for at least ; with bleeding, tenderness, contractions or abnormal FHR, extend observation, commonly .
  • ✎Rh-negative trauma: give RhIG, ideally within 72 h — standard later-pregnancy dose , which covers up to of fetal whole blood (15 mL fetal red cells); quantify fetomaternal hemorrhage (Kleihauer-Betke) and give additional 300 µg vials if the bleed is larger (ACOG 2017).

tap to flip

Placental abruption.

💉PPH — First Response, Uterotonics & Tranexamic Acid11 items▾

Recall
Heavy postpartum bleeding — what is done IMMEDIATELY?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING EMERGENCY THERAPY: IV access + crystalloid/blood resuscitation + uterine massage + hemorrhage protocol — simultaneously with identifying the cause (Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin).
PPH drug ladder (uterine atony)
PriorityDrugTestable doseRestriction / pearlAnswer
FIRST-LINE (life-saving)Oxytocin (IV oxytocin is the first intervention) + vigorous uterine massage10 IU IM or slow IV (WHO 2025), or IV infusion 20 IU in 1 L crystalloid (e.g., LR; WHO regimen runs it over 2 h, with a further 5–10 IU slow IV when required). ACOG 2017: 10–40 U in 500–1,000 mL as IV infusion, or 10 U IMFew postpartum contraindications; avoid rapid IV bolus
ALTERNATIVEMethylergonovine0.2 mg (200 µg) IM, may repeat every 2–4 h (ACOG 2017)CONTRAINDICATED in HTN / preeclampsia — severe vasoconstriction / hypertension
ALTERNATIVECarboprost (PGF₂α)250 µg IM, may repeat every 15–90 min, maximum 8 doses = 2 mg (ACOG 2017)CONTRAINDICATED in asthma — bronchospasm
ALTERNATIVEMisoprostol800 µg sublingual (WHO / FIGO); ACOG 2017: 600–1,000 µg oral, sublingual or rectal. Classic textbook: 800–1,000 µg PRUseful when injectable uterotonics are unavailable; not subject to the asthma/HTN-specific contraindications
Adjunct (current WHO; life-saving)Tranexamic acid1 g IV over 10 min within 3 h of birth; repeat 1 g after 30 min if bleeding continues, or if it restarts within 24 hNot a substitute for uterotonics / control of the bleeding site
  • ✎First-line uterotonic for atony: oxytocin IM, or in 1 L crystalloid IV — always with uterine massage.
Recall
Current WHO oxytocin regimen for PPH?
tap to flip
Answer
10 IU slow IV or IM; infusion 20 IU in 1 L crystalloid over 2 h, with 5–10 IU slow IV when required. Avoid rapid IV bolus. Further oxytocin / misoprostol / ergometrine as appropriate.
  • ✎Alternative uterotonics: methylergonovine IM, carboprost IM, misoprostol sublingual or rectal.
Board trap · Uterotonic contraindicationsClassic wrong choices: methylergonovine is CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension or preeclampsia (severe vasoconstriction, can markedly raise BP; current WHO guidance likewise bars ergometrine in hypertensive disorders); carboprost is CONTRAINDICATED in asthma (bronchospasm). Give methylergonovine only if no HTN, carboprost only if no asthma.
Board trap · “Contraindicated in pregnancy”?The methylergonovine–hypertension and carboprost–asthma rules are maternal, condition-specific contraindications — not universal pregnancy contraindications and not fetal contraindications.
  • ★Uterotonic order: uterine massage + oxytocin → methylergonovine → carboprost / misoprostol → procedural escalation. For persistent atony, add each uterotonic according to the patient’s contraindications.
  • ✎Tranexamic acid in PPH: IV over 10 min within of birth; repeat 1 g after if bleeding continues, or if it restarts within 24 h.
Board trap · Tranexamic acidTXA is an early adjunct, not a substitute for uterotonics and control of the bleeding site. Avoid when there is a clear antifibrinolytic contraindication, such as a known thromboembolic event during pregnancy (thrombotic risk).
🩺 Think it through
After a vaginal delivery, a woman with preeclampsia and asthma has a boggy uterus and heavy bleeding that continues despite uterine massage and oxytocin. Which uterotonic comes next?
Misoprostol 800 µg (sublingual or rectal) — it carries neither the hypertension nor the asthma restriction. Methylergonovine is the wrong choice in hypertension/preeclampsia and carboprost is the wrong choice in asthma. Give TXA early and escalate to balloon / surgery / hysterectomy if bleeding persists.

Beyond drugs — procedural escalation
SituationInterventionKey pointAnswer

Board trap · Refractory PPH — escalate, do not delayTempting: persisting with repeated drugs. Right — in uncontrolled, life-threatening hemorrhage do not delay; escalate rapidly: Bakri balloon tamponade / uterine artery embolization → laparotomy with uterine-sparing surgery — O’Leary ligation / B-Lynch (vessel ligation / compression surgery) → hysterectomy = LIFE-SAVING definitive treatment if uncontrolled.
  • ★Uterine inversion: LIFE-SAVING — resuscitate simultaneously for hemorrhagic/vasovagal shock → FIRST-LINE: immediate manual uterine replacement with firm cephalad pressure toward the fundus → if replacement is difficult, relax the uterus (nitroglycerin or halogenated general anesthesia) → failed manual replacement: laparotomy and surgical replacement → after reduction, stop relaxants and treat the associated uterine atony / PPH aggressively.

🧭Exam Blueprint, Method Classes & Choosing a Method8 items▾

  • ★Exam weight: 3% / 3 items — 1 Understanding, 1 Application, 1 Analysis. Expected skills: classify contraceptive methods, differentiate mechanisms and short-/long-term adverse effects, and select the right method for the right patient while recognizing precautions and contraindications.
Classification of contraceptive methods
CategoryMethodsAnswer
NaturalPeriodic abstinence, withdrawal, lactational amenorrhea (LAM)
BarrierMale/internal condom, diaphragm, cervical cap, spermicide
LARCCopper IUD, LNG-IUD, etonogestrel implant
Combined hormonalPill, patch, vaginal ring
Progestin-onlyPOP, DMPA, implant, LNG-IUD
EmergencyLevonorgestrel EC, ulipristal, copper IUD
PermanentTubal sterilization, vasectomy
Recall
Which methods have the lowest failure rates, and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Those with the least user dependence: IUDs, implants and sterilization. IUD/implant = the most effective reversible choices with least user error (if no condition-specific contraindication); LARC is a first-line postpartum strategy.
  • ★Board decision sequence: exclude pregnancy when relevant → define reproductive goals → assess breastfeeding/postpartum status → screen for estrogen contraindications, infection, uterine distortion, cancer, thrombotic risk and interacting drugs → prioritize efficacy/adherence → counsel on bleeding pattern, return to fertility, STI protection and permanence.
  • ★Method-selection algorithm: exclude pregnancy when relevant → STI protection needed? → condoms → screen for estrogen contraindications → estrogen contraindicated: Cu-IUD, LNG-IUD, implant, DMPA or appropriate POP according to MEC → heavy menses/anemia: favor LNG-IUD or hormonal suppression rather than copper IUD → wants lowest user error: IUD/implant → desires pregnancy soon: avoid methods with delayed return to fertility such as DMPA if that delay is unacceptable → completed family: offer permanent contraception only after thorough informed-consent counseling.
Recall
Couple for whom avoiding pregnancy is critical, currently using a natural/barrier method → advice?
tap to flip
Answer
Move from user-dependent natural/barrier methods to LARC or permanent contraception.
🩺 Think it through
A 38-year-old smoker with migraine with aura asks for contraception. What do you offer?
Avoid CHC. Choose a progestin-only method or a non-estrogen LARC after MEC review.
  • ★Device durations and failure rates are given here per current labelling and CDC 2024 / US MEC 2024; where an older figure is still met in textbooks and old board questions it is added as a brief “Classic textbook” note.

🤱Natural Family Planning & Lactational Amenorrhea8 items▾

Recall
Natural methods — which are they, and how reliable?
tap to flip
Answer
Periodic abstinence, withdrawal (coitus interruptus) and lactational amenorrhea. They are the least reliable methods when pregnancy prevention is a high priority.
Recall
Periodic abstinence — how is the fertile window identified?
tap to flip
Answer
Menstrual timing, cervical mucus, basal body temperature, ovulation symptoms or ovulation-prediction testing — it infers the fertile window from the cyclic changes around ovulation and does not suppress ovulation.
  • ✎Periodic abstinence (fertility-awareness methods) works best only with regular cycles and a highly motivated couple who identify the fertile window and abstain appropriately; typical-use failure is depending on the method (CDC 2024). Classic textbook: effectiveness about 55%–80%.
Recall
Mechanism of lactational amenorrhea?
tap to flip
Answer
Elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic pulsatile GnRH → ovulation is delayed after delivery.
🧠 Memory toolLAM — all three criteria must hold
1Exclusive breastfeeding
2Continued amenorrhea
3≤6 months postpartum (maximum duration = 6 months)
Usable only while ALL three remain true.
Recall
When must a LAM user switch or add another method?
tap to flip
Answer
As soon as any criterion is lost: menses returns, supplementation begins, or the infant reaches 6 months. LAM does not harm breastfeeding and supports infant exposure to breast milk, but must not continue as sole contraception beyond the strict window.
Board trap · Amenorrhea ≠ infertileOvulation may return before the first postpartum menses, so amenorrhea alone outside the strict LAM criteria does not reliably exclude fertility. Casual reliance on breastfeeding is unreliable: about 50% of lactating mothers begin to ovulate between 6 and 12 months after delivery, even while still breastfeeding.
🩺 Think it through
A woman 2 months postpartum is amenorrheic and exclusively breastfeeding. Can she rely on breastfeeding for contraception?
Yes — LAM can work temporarily, but counsel a transition plan to another method before 6 months.

🛡️Barrier Methods: Condoms, Diaphragm, Cap & Spermicide8 items▾

Recall
How do barrier methods work?
tap to flip
Answer
They prevent sperm from reaching the cervix/upper reproductive tract without altering ovarian function.
Barrier devices compared
DeviceHow it works / placementProblemsLimitsAnswer
Male condomMechanical sperm barrierLatex/lubricant irritationNo systemic contraindication
Internal (female) condomLines the vaginal canal, with an external ring——
Diaphragm + spermicideSits over the cervix; cervical barrier used with spermicideUTI/bladder irritation, latex/spermicide hypersensitivity, rare toxic shock syndrome if retained too longInability to fit/use; spermicide concern in those at high HIV risk
Cervical capSeals directly over the cervix by suctionPoorer efficacy in parous womenRefit after pregnancy or major weight change
Recall
Which contraceptives protect against HIV/STI transmission?
tap to flip
Answer
Condoms only (male and internal) — first-line whenever STI protection is required and the best method for reducing STI transmission, giving STI protection + contraception. Hormonal methods (implant, pills, injection) and IUDs (copper or LNG) give no STI protection; diaphragms, caps and spermicides are primarily contraceptive barriers. If STI prevention is wanted → condom regardless of any additional method.
  • ✎Diaphragm: place with spermicide before intercourse, then leave in for at least hours after intercourse and never more than hours in total (current labelling; avoid early removal, and prolonged retention risks toxic shock syndrome).
Recall
Diaphragm in place and intercourse is repeated within 6–8 hours → what to do?
tap to flip
Answer
Add more spermicide without removing the device.
  • ✎Diaphragm: replace about every years; refit after pregnancy and after a body-weight change of more than %.
  • ✎Cervical cap: may be inserted up to hours before intercourse, is left for at least 6 hours afterwards, and may remain in place no longer than (classic textbook: 1–2 days).
Board trap · Spermicide aloneRelatively weak contraception and does NOT protect against STIs. Frequent nonoxynol-9 exposure may irritate vaginal mucosa and potentially increase susceptibility to infection.

🧷IUDs: Copper vs Levonorgestrel — Mechanism & Choice9 items▾

Recall
Mechanism of the copper IUD?
tap to flip
Answer
A local sterile (spermicidal) inflammatory response that impairs sperm function, motility and fertilization. IUDs do not suppress ovulation.
Recall
What does the LNG-IUD add to the basic IUD effect?
tap to flip
Answer
Progestin-mediated cervical-mucus thickening and endometrial atrophy, on top of the local inflammatory effect.
Board trap · IUD ≠ abortifacientFertilization needs viable sperm to cross cervical mucus and the uterus to reach the tube; IUDs act mainly on sperm/fertilization — they are not abortifacients.
Copper IUD vs LNG-IUD
FeatureCopper IUD (ParaGard)LNG-IUD (Mirena)Answer
HormoneNone — highly effective nonhormonal methodLevonorgestrel — highly effective
Menstrual effect↑ bleeding and cramping; may worsen dysmenorrhea/menorrhagiaIrregular bleeding at first → lighter flow / amenorrhea (amenorrhea in ~15%–20%)
Choose whenA highly effective nonhormonal method is desiredContraception plus less heavy bleeding/dysmenorrhea is wanted — advantageous in anemia/heavy menstrual bleeding; heavy periods + wants LARC → LNG-IUD rather than copper
Other side effectsExpulsion, perforation—
Approved duration (current labelling)10 years8 years for the 52-mg device (FDA 2022). Classic textbook: 5 years
🧠 Memory toolBleeding contrast pair
CuCopper = Cramps and heavier menses
LNGLevonorgestrel = Lighter menses → amenorrhea
  • ✎Cumulative failure: ParaGard about at 10 years; Mirena about at 5 years.
Recall
What are IUD strings for?
tap to flip
Answer
Two strings extend through the cervix: they allow placement checks (detecting expulsion/migration) and facilitate later removal.
  • ★Copper T and LNG-IUD are both T-shaped devices passed through the cervical canal into the endometrial cavity; perforation and expulsion are complications of placement, not contraceptive mechanisms.
Recall
Return to fertility after IUD removal?
tap to flip
Answer
Generally returns after removal — neither copper nor LNG-IUD permanently suppresses ovarian function. A history of IUD use requires no delay before attempting pregnancy.

tap to flip

Exclude pregnancy (pregnancy test), assess STI/cervicitis risk with gonorrhea/chlamydia testing when clinically appropriate (chlamydial cervicitis is often asymptomatic — screen by STI risk), and assess uterine anatomy.

Recall
Complications of IUDs?
tap to flip
